full_text:
Interviewer:	What course is it that you’re doing?

Subject:	Music technology.

Interviewer:	Music technology. The research that we’re doing, it’s mainly looking at engineering, I don’t know whether you’d consider your course to be related to engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I suppose it is. Yes, somehow.

Interviewer:	We’re mainly looking at engineering as a – like a male dominated industry and looking at how women get on in the industry and trying to improve the situation for women. So that’s what it’s about and I’ve just got some questions about your course and why you decided to do your course.

Subject:	Okay.

Interviewer:	Okay. Did you do A Levels?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What A Levels did you do?

Subject:	Um, well, I did them in [country] so they’re slightly different. So I did, um, English, Irish, Maths, Geography, French, um, Home Economics and Business.

Interviewer:	That sounds like loads.

Subject:	Yeah. They’re not as complicated as A Levels though, so it’s slightly – they’re slightly less detailed.

Interviewer:	Okay. What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Um, it was a community college.

Interviewer:	It wasn’t like a girls’ school or anything like that?

Subject:	No, it was a mixed – mixed school.

Interviewer:	Have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	Um, not directly related to electronics. Um, I’ve done a few live sound recordings and stuff like that, but not full time or anything like that.

Interviewer:	Okay. What do your parents do? Do either of them do anything similar to what you want to do?

Subject:	Um, they’re both musicians, but my mum’s a teacher and my dad is a managing director. So they don’t work with music, but they – they just kind of – they play um…

Interviewer:	Okay. When and why do you think that you decided to do music technology?

Subject:	Um, I wasn’t going to do it for years and then I applied for loads of courses and then realised that the only thing I wanted to do was music, so I had to come here to do it because they can’t do it in Ireland. So I said yeah, because I knew if I did something else I’d regret not doing music.

Interviewer:	What do you think it is about music that appeals to you?

Subject:	Um, the critical side I like a lot and also the producing side, so I came in wanting to be a producer but that’s slightly changed a bit, I don’t really know what I want to do anymore. Um, yeah, I still don’t really know what I want to do.

Interviewer:	Okay. I’ll ask you a bit more about that later on. Do you think that the fact that your parents are both musicians influenced you at all?

Subject:	Yeah, because I was taught music from a young age anyway, so I didn’t really, well, I had a choice, but I was going to learn music whatever and then, yeah, so they’ve had – they have had an influence on it because they’re both musicians.

Interviewer:	Okay. Did you do any career research at all before you started?

Subject:	Um, I kind of had an idea of what you could go into, like sound engineering and producing and stuff like that, but I suppose you don’t realise, well, with music how little work there is really until you come to university. Not how little work there is but how you’re going to have to do a lot of other things before you can get to where you want to be.

Interviewer:	Okay, how did you decide to come to [university] then?

Subject:	Um, I just applied to a few universities and – for music technology because not that many places do it, um, and these were the first people to send me a letter to come for an open day, so I came here first and I couldn’t afford to fly every time I was offered an open day so, I liked it here so I said ‘Why not?’.

Interviewer:	Okay. Is your degree course – is it mostly males on your course?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you know that before you started?

Subject:	Yeah, because I’d done, um, I did a year’s course before I came here in sound engineering and I was the only girl then. Um, I thought there’d be slightly more but there isn’t, it’s still…

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	No, because I knew it before I was going into it; it doesn’t really bother me.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do it?

Subject:	I think so, yeah. I don’t think they, um… I think when something has ‘technology’ at the end of it people get put off and realise that… they think it’s like all technology and stuff like that, when it’s not really. It’s a good mixture of things.

Interviewer:	Do you think people think technology is like getting your hands dirty and stuff?

Subject:	Yeah, I think that’s what they associate it with and it’s… my course isn’t really a lot of that at all.

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done then to get more women into it?

Subject:	Um, I think a different label could be put on the course, because I think if people knew what we studied they’d be more inclined to do it. Like we do performance studies and pop music studies and stuff like that, and I think women have an interest in that and if they were shown that that’s part of the course I think they’d do it.

Interviewer:	Okay. What characteristics do you think make a good music technician?

Subject:	Um, I suppose you have to have a lot of knowledge and you have to be very dedicated for like overnight sessions in studios and stuff like that, and to an extent I think people let it kind of take over quite a lot of their lives in like they’re willing to spend as many hours as possible in the studios and stuff like that, whereas an office job is nine to five and that’s it. And I think people take their work home, but that’s probably because they enjoy it a lot. So I think – I think you need people skills as well to deal with… to deal with musicians and engineers and other people like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or female characteristics?

Subject:	Um, I think males probably are better at, I don’t know, mixing with different people. I think they’re probably less… I don’t know, judgemental when it comes to certain things than females, but I don’t think there’s that big of a difference really.

Interviewer:	Do you think, you said about spending loads of time in the studio and stuff, do you think that could be a reason why less women go into it, like if they’ve got other family commitments and stuff like that?

Subject:	Definitely, because if you want to… if you want to make it quite big and, you know, get your career off to a start you have to be willing to at least spend a few years with that being the only thing in your mind really. So if you’ve got like you’re starting a family or something like that, there’s no way you’ll have time to properly start your career.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you at all?

Subject:	Not really, no. No, because I think if I really want to do it then I will do it. I don’t think… I don’t know, I don’t think I have the dedication of some people, like spending all night in the studios and stuff like that, but I still think it’s what I want to do, so I’m willing to do it.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male dominated environment?

Subject:	Um, I suppose the advantage is that people remember you. Going for interviews or stuff like that they remember you as being the girl, because there’s only one girl usually, one or two. Um, disadvantage is I’m not saying that people are sexist but I think they do have preconceived ideas about women and technology, that we’re just not good at it. I think, um… I do think they still have that, not bad but there’s a couple of people, well, in my class there’s a couple of people who I know still think that women shouldn’t be messing around with technology and stuff like that. But, um…

Interviewer:	How does that make you feel?

Subject:	I don’t mind because if – if I was… unconfident in how I could do things then it would make me feel a bit paranoid and stuff, like oh God I can’t do it and they’re going to think it’s because I’m a girl, but I can do a lot of the things and I’m quite confident in how I do them, so it doesn’t really bother me. And it’s only a couple of people; most people don’t even notice any more.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you have to work harder at all to prove yourself, or…?

Subject:	Slightly, because I think because I’m a girl I'm more determined not to mess up because I think instead of them thinking, ‘Oh she just messed up’ they’ll think ‘Well she messed up and she’s a girl, so that’s probably why she’s messed up’. So I think slightly harder, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay. Has the degree been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Um… yes and no. It was – there was a lot of stuff involved in the degree that we weren’t made aware of before we went in, like a lot of multimedia, um, stuff that we – that nobody really wanted to do in the course, but we’ve done it now and – I’m in the third year and you get to decide basically what you want to do in third year, so you can just specify what you want, which is a lot better. But first and second year there was a lot of things that we didn’t really like.

Interviewer:	And you’d rather have done different things?

Subject:	Yeah, but looking at it now I can see why it was worthwhile to do those things, but a little bit more time spent on music would have been better, I think, for everyone.

Interviewer:	Okay. What do you think have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Um, the best things are working in the studio with other musicians on the performance side of things. Um, I love critical studies as well, which is just talking about music and arguing about it and… that was one of the most enjoyable ones because, I mean you get to talk about music with people who love to talk about music, that kind of thing, whereas your friends get bored when you talk about music all the time. So that was – that’s probably one of the best bits.

Interviewer:	Okay, and what about the worst?

Subject:	The worst, um, doing a lot of multimedia that I knew I would never want to do again. That I’d never – I wouldn’t use it again and I would never think about a career in that field but yet I still had to do it to pass.

Interviewer:	Okay. Are you pleased that you did choose this course?

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah definitely.

Interviewer:	Okay, good. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	One, yeah.

Interviewer:	Have you noticed any difference in the sort of type of subject that the female taught or…?

Subject:	Yeah, because she taught me business and, um, a music cultures thing in first year, music cultures module, so it wasn’t to do with technology at all, it was the opposite side of things.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think it would be encouraging to have more female lecturers, or doesn’t it bother you?

Subject:	Um, I’d like to see a female in the studio at some point. I’ve never seen a female lecturer in the studio at all. Um, or in any of the electronic side of things there’s never any females about. But, um, it would be encouraging. I’d like to see how men would react to a woman showing them how to use the technology. But, um, I don’t know when that’s going to happen.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that the female lecturer treated you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Um, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the male lecturers treat you the same as the male students?

Subject:	Um, I think so, yeah. I haven’t really noticed or thought about it really. Yeah, they do, they do.

Interviewer:	Okay. Have you got a personal tutor at all?

Subject:	Yes, but I don’t know who it is. I know we all have one but I don’t think anyone checks.

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anyone else that you go to for like advice about either personal or academic…?

Subject:	Yeah, there’s a couple of lecturers who are very approachable because we’ve known them since first year and done practical stuff with them, so they’d be… yeah, they are approachable.

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anyone or anything that you’d say has been like the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Um… I don’t really know. The female lecturer I have, [name], is very good and she’s – she’s kind of got her hands in a lot of things, like the business side of things and the, um, composing side of things and publishing side of things, which I’d like to do, to have kind of all them things going at the same time. So, there hasn’t been one major thing though.

Interviewer:	Yeah, just bits of…

Subject:	Yeah, just bits of things.

Interviewer:	Okay. Have you had to do much group work?

Subject:	Yeah, loads.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Um, it depends on your group really. It’s good when you get to choose your group, but –

Interviewer:	How often do you get to choose?

Subject:	Rarely. You get to choose kind of who you work with musically. When we had to do our compositions and stuff we chose people who we worked with musically, but, um, for other things, like we’ve a group project this year which is, um, a third of our whole degree, which we think is far too much because you’re relying on a lot of other people for a third of your degree. So, I don’t mind doing it, but as long as you have a good group, because if you don’t have a good group then they could take down a lot of your marks, which is slightly unfair.

Interviewer:	Are there many other women on your course?

Subject:	There is one who’s doing music tech and then there’s one who’s doing sound technology. Um, I think that’s it.

Interviewer:	Do you – have you worked with them in groups before?

Subject:	I’m working with [name] at the moment, who does sound technology in, um, a group and I worked with [name], the other girl, in, um, when we did compositions. 

Interviewer:	Do you prefer working with male or female students or don’t you think it makes a difference? Do you think they bring different characteristics to the group?

Subject:	Um, they are different, yeah. It doesn’t really bother me working with either. I think females sometimes are better academically or less laid back when it comes to getting things done academically, but when it comes to music I think they’re both equal.

Interviewer:	Okay. Have you had particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Um, no. One group performance we were all very nervous because it was our first time performing in front of people, but never really a bad experience.

Interviewer:	Yeah, when things have gone wrong it’s just been because people aren’t putting the same amount of effort?

Subject:	Yeah, that’s the only thing that goes wrong really, is when people are just lazy.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. You’ve not gone or been on placement have you?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Did you have the opportunity to go on a placement?

Subject:	Yeah, last year they, um, I could have been doing it this year and then come back this year again, but the placements they were offering us were completely nothing to do with our side of things. It was, um, it was basically a factory work that had small relation to electronics somewhere, but nothing to do with music or anything like that. So everyone – a lot of people didn’t do it.

Interviewer:	There just weren’t the opportunities. If there had been something –

Subject:	If there had been something which really interests me I think probably yeah, but the other thing was the cost, that we still had to pay for being in the University even though we’d be out working, and that put a lot of people off. And the fact that they’d probably have to move to London or somewhere like that, so it’d be more expensive.

Interviewer:	Okay. You said you’d got a bit of work experience, have you enjoyed doing that?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’ll help you when you go to get a job afterwards?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. I think experience is probably more important than a degree when it comes to my – music technology, but I just wanted to do the degree anyway. But, um, the experience is very important.

Interviewer:	Okay. What do you think have been the best and worst things about your work experience so far?

Subject:	Um, the best thing is when everything goes right and everything sounds great when you’re doing live sound. The worst thing is when something goes wrong and everybody knows that something’s gone wrong because they can hear it, but, um, I haven’t – I’ve been lucky, I haven’t had that much bad experience.

Interviewer:	Have you brought anything like from your experience back to university that’s helped you on the course at all?

Subject:	Um, yeah, I mean stuff in the studio, if something goes wrong you know initially where to look for what’s gone wrong, that kind of a thing. But we don’t do that much live sound, so only bits, but yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that the educational experience or the way that you’re taught reflects what it’s like in industry at all?

Subject:	Um, yeah, I do, because people – the people who teach us generally have been working in the industry, so they’ve got a lot of knowledge about it and stuff, but the studios maybe are a little less professional than what you would be working with and things wouldn’t go wrong as often and stuff like that, because, well, there’s a lot of students and very little studios, so obviously things go wrong, but I don’t think – I think the lecturers have a lot of experience, so they tell us all the time what the stuff is really like.

Interviewer:	Do you do a lot of practical work?

Subject:	Yeah, a lot.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you finish?

Subject:	Um, I don’t really know. Um, I’d like to get into the business – the business side of things somehow, the industry side of things. But where I’ll start I don’t really know. I haven’t got a clue.

Interviewer:	What sort of things do you think will attract you to a company? Will it just be the type of work that they do when you’ve decided what you want to do? Will you look at things like training opportunities and salary and stuff like that?

Subject:	I think yeah, things like that. It will be the type of work I want to do, I think. I think salary, I mean it is important but it’s not what I’m going to look for. That’ll just be a bonus if it happens to be good, but yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay. How do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	God, um, a lot. I think, yeah, I mean I work in the summers so it’s not going to be a big shock to work, but, um, to work in something that I really, really want to do is going to take a lot of dedication and stuff, whereas the university is very relaxed and chilled out and stuff like that. So it is – it is going to be a bit of a shock.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll actually use what you’re doing now?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so, because we’ve – they’ve made sure that the course does quite a lot of things, like the business side, the multimedia side and stuff like that. I don’t know how much I’m going to use, but I’m sure some of it will be useful.

Interviewer:	Okay. What are you most looking forward to about working in industry?

Subject:	Um, I suppose doing what I want to do really. Um, I’d like to run my own thing eventually, to be able to make my own music and I’d like to do my own business side of things as well, but mainly just being able to make music, yeah.

Interviewer:	Is there anything that you’re apprehensive about or anything?

Subject:	Um, the money side of things because it’s going to take a long time to start earning money and then paying back debts and stuff like that. It’s going to be for a couple of years really hard to cope with, money, but I’ll be all right.

Interviewer:	Okay. Would you like to work abroad or travel at all?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m planning to travel when I leave here.

Interviewer:	And work at the same time, or just…?

Subject:	Yeah, travel for a couple of months and then work. Um, and I don’t know what kind of work I’m looking for. I think I’ll probably just work wherever and then think about a career when I come back here, but yeah I’m planning to travel next year.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that the career prospects are good in music technology?

Subject:	Um, I think they’re growing, especially in [area] and around [town] because there’s so many new studios opening up and there’s so much music coming from this part of the country. Um, London is still the place to go really if you want to work in it, because there’s so many studios there. I think the UK is good for opportunities, yeah. [Country] is not as good, I think that’s why I'm going to have to stay here, but, um, it’s quite good, yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you like to stay around here?

Subject:	Around [area], yeah, I wouldn’t mind staying around here. It depends what comes up in [town] and stuff like that, but the opportunities are quite good as well, which…

Interviewer:	Okay. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m glad I decided to do this course and stuff.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	Um, I think if I’d known how much multimedia was involved in this I might have chosen a different course, but I’m still glad that I did it. They’ve got new courses now, like pop music and stuff, which I probably would have chosen had I known how much multimedia was in this course, but I’m glad I did it.

Interviewer:	Okay. I’ve nearly finished, but I’ve got a difficult question now. What five words would you use to describe like the culture or the characteristics of your field?

Subject:	The characteristics of my field, like music technology?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Um, hard work, you need to be dedicated. Um, you need to have good personal skills with people and be creative as well; people underestimate how creative you actually need to be. Um, I think that’s it.

Interviewer:	Would you describe it as male dominated or is that –

Subject:	Very male dominated, yeah.

Interviewer:	But would that be one of the things that came into your head if you had to describe it?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it would have been but I don’t even think about it any more, I’m just so used to being the only girl a lot of the time, which I don’t mind, but, yeah, it is extremely male dominated.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it’ll stay like that or do you think the situation will improve for women?

Subject:	I think – I think it’s going to stay like that for a while unless things are done to change the image of the course and stuff like that. But I think technology, yeah, it’s still going to stay a lot of men involved. I think bit by bit women are going to start doing it, but not for a few years I don’t think.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact that it’s male dominated will cause you any problems in the future at all?

Subject:	It may do. I don’t pretend that it won’t because… I just think that there is people out there who will still have preconceptions because I'm a girl that I’m going to be good at certain things and not so good at certain things. So it all depends on, I think, the attitude of your employer and the attitude of the people you work with. I think the worst way that it’s going to come across is when people expect you to be a man when they hire you or go into a studio and expect to be working with a male engineer. I think their attitudes will probably be the worst, more than an employer, to you. I just think when a band will come in, say, four males in a rock band and expect to be working with a male engineer and then I think when they see a woman they’ll be a bit like that, but not for employers I don’t think.

Interviewer:	Okay. That’s everything, thank you very much.

Subject:	Okay, thanks.

Interviewer:	Thank you.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think a different label could be put on the course, because I think if people knew what we studied they’d be more inclined to do it. Like we do performance studies and pop music studies and stuff like that, and I think women have an interest in that and if they were shown that that’s part of the course I think they’d do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What characteristics do you think make a good music technician?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I suppose you have to have a lot of knowledge and you have to be very dedicated for like overnight sessions in studios and stuff like that, and to an extent I think people let it kind of take over quite a lot of their lives in like they’re willing to spend as many hours as possible in the studios and stuff like that, whereas an office job is nine to five and that’s it. And I think people take their work home, but that’s probably because they enjoy it a lot. So I think – I think you need people skills as well to deal with… to deal with musicians and engineers and other people like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think males probably are better at, I don’t know, mixing with different people. I think they’re probably less… I don’t know, judgemental when it comes to certain things than females, but I don’t think there’s that big of a difference really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think, you said about spending loads of time in the studio and stuff, do you think that could be a reason why less women go into it, like if they’ve got other family commitments and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, because if you want to… if you want to make it quite big and, you know, get your career off to a start you have to be willing to at least spend a few years with that being the only thing in your mind really. So if you’ve got like you’re starting a family or something like that, there’s no way you’ll have time to properly start your career.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, no. No, because I think if I really want to do it then I will do it. I don’t think… I don’t know, I don’t think I have the dedication of some people, like spending all night in the studios and stuff like that, but I still think it’s what I want to do, so I’m willing to do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male dominated environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I suppose the advantage is that people remember you. Going for interviews or stuff like that they remember you as being the girl, because there’s only one girl usually, one or two. Um, disadvantage is I’m not saying that people are sexist but I think they do have preconceived ideas about women and technology, that we’re just not good at it. I think, um… I do think they still have that, not bad but there’s a couple of people, well, in my class there’s a couple of people who I know still think that women shouldn’t be messing around with technology and stuff like that. But, um…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How does that make you feel?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t mind because if – if I was… unconfident in how I could do things then it would make me feel a bit paranoid and stuff, like oh God I can’t do it and they’re going to think it’s because I’m a girl, but I can do a lot of the things and I’m quite confident in how I do them, so it doesn’t really bother me. And it’s only a couple of people; most people don’t even notice any more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you have to work harder at all to prove yourself, or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Slightly, because I think because I’m a girl I'm more determined not to mess up because I think instead of them thinking, ‘Oh she just messed up’ they’ll think ‘Well she messed up and she’s a girl, so that’s probably why she’s messed up’. So I think slightly harder, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Has the degree been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um… yes and no. It was – there was a lot of stuff involved in the degree that we weren’t made aware of before we went in, like a lot of multimedia, um, stuff that we – that nobody really wanted to do in the course, but we’ve done it now and – I’m in the third year and you get to decide basically what you want to do in third year, so you can just specify what you want, which is a lot better. But first and second year there was a lot of things that we didn’t really like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And you’d rather have done different things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but looking at it now I can see why it was worthwhile to do those things, but a little bit more time spent on music would have been better, I think, for everyone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What do you think have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, the best things are working in the studio with other musicians on the performance side of things. Um, I love critical studies as well, which is just talking about music and arguing about it and… that was one of the most enjoyable ones because, I mean you get to talk about music with people who love to talk about music, that kind of thing, whereas your friends get bored when you talk about music all the time. So that was – that’s probably one of the best bits.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and what about the worst?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The worst, um, doing a lot of multimedia that I knew I would never want to do again. That I’d never – I wouldn’t use it again and I would never think about a career in that field but yet I still had to do it to pass.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Are you pleased that you did choose this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Yeah definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, good. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you noticed any difference in the sort of type of subject that the female taught or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because she taught me business and, um, a music cultures thing in first year, music cultures module, so it wasn’t to do with technology at all, it was the opposite side of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think it would be encouraging to have more female lecturers, or doesn’t it bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I’d like to see a female in the studio at some point. I’ve never seen a female lecturer in the studio at all. Um, or in any of the electronic side of things there’s never any females about. But, um, it would be encouraging. I’d like to see how men would react to a woman showing them how to use the technology. But, um, I don’t know when that’s going to happen.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that the female lecturer treated you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male lecturers treat you the same as the male students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think so, yeah. I haven’t really noticed or thought about it really. Yeah, they do, they do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Have you got a personal tutor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but I don’t know who it is. I know we all have one but I don’t think anyone checks.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anyone else that you go to for like advice about either personal or academic…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there’s a couple of lecturers who are very approachable because we’ve known them since first year and done practical stuff with them, so they’d be… yeah, they are approachable.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anyone or anything that you’d say has been like the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um… I don’t really know. The female lecturer I have, [name], is very good and she’s – she’s kind of got her hands in a lot of things, like the business side of things and the, um, composing side of things and publishing side of things, which I’d like to do, to have kind of all them things going at the same time. So, there hasn’t been one major thing though.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, just bits of…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just bits of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Have you had to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, loads.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it depends on your group really. It’s good when you get to choose your group, but –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How often do you get to choose?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Rarely. You get to choose kind of who you work with musically. When we had to do our compositions and stuff we chose people who we worked with musically, but, um, for other things, like we’ve a group project this year which is, um, a third of our whole degree, which we think is far too much because you’re relying on a lot of other people for a third of your degree. So, I don’t mind doing it, but as long as you have a good group, because if you don’t have a good group then they could take down a lot of your marks, which is slightly unfair.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there many other women on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There is one who’s doing music tech and then there’s one who’s doing sound technology. Um, I think that’s it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you – have you worked with them in groups before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m working with [name] at the moment, who does sound technology in, um, a group and I worked with [name], the other girl, in, um, when we did compositions.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer working with male or female students or don’t you think it makes a difference? Do you think they bring different characteristics to the group?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, they are different, yeah. It doesn’t really bother me working with either. I think females sometimes are better academically or less laid back when it comes to getting things done academically, but when it comes to music I think they’re both equal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Have you had particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no. One group performance we were all very nervous because it was our first time performing in front of people, but never really a bad experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, when things have gone wrong it’s just been because people aren’t putting the same amount of effort?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, that’s the only thing that goes wrong really, is when people are just lazy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. You’ve not gone or been on placement have you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have the opportunity to go on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, last year they, um, I could have been doing it this year and then come back this year again, but the placements they were offering us were completely nothing to do with our side of things. It was, um, it was basically a factory work that had small relation to electronics somewhere, but nothing to do with music or anything like that. So everyone – a lot of people didn’t do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: There just weren’t the opportunities. If there had been something –

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If there had been something which really interests me I think probably yeah, but the other thing was the cost, that we still had to pay for being in the University even though we’d be out working, and that put a lot of people off. And the fact that they’d probably have to move to London or somewhere like that, so it’d be more expensive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. You said you’d got a bit of work experience, have you enjoyed doing that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’ll help you when you go to get a job afterwards?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I think experience is probably more important than a degree when it comes to my – music technology, but I just wanted to do the degree anyway. But, um, the experience is very important.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What do you think have been the best and worst things about your work experience so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, the best thing is when everything goes right and everything sounds great when you’re doing live sound. The worst thing is when something goes wrong and everybody knows that something’s gone wrong because they can hear it, but, um, I haven’t – I’ve been lucky, I haven’t had that much bad experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you brought anything like from your experience back to university that’s helped you on the course at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah, I mean stuff in the studio, if something goes wrong you know initially where to look for what’s gone wrong, that kind of a thing. But we don’t do that much live sound, so only bits, but yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that the educational experience or the way that you’re taught reflects what it’s like in industry at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah, I do, because people – the people who teach us generally have been working in the industry, so they’ve got a lot of knowledge about it and stuff, but the studios maybe are a little less professional than what you would be working with and things wouldn’t go wrong as often and stuff like that, because, well, there’s a lot of students and very little studios, so obviously things go wrong, but I don’t think – I think the lecturers have a lot of experience, so they tell us all the time what the stuff is really like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you do a lot of practical work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t really know. Um, I’d like to get into the business – the business side of things somehow, the industry side of things. But where I’ll start I don’t really know. I haven’t got a clue.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of things do you think will attract you to a company? Will it just be the type of work that they do when you’ve decided what you want to do? Will you look at things like training opportunities and salary and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think yeah, things like that. It will be the type of work I want to do, I think. I think salary, I mean it is important but it’s not what I’m going to look for. That’ll just be a bonus if it happens to be good, but yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. How do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: God, um, a lot. I think, yeah, I mean I work in the summers so it’s not going to be a big shock to work, but, um, to work in something that I really, really want to do is going to take a lot of dedication and stuff, whereas the university is very relaxed and chilled out and stuff like that. So it is – it is going to be a bit of a shock.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll actually use what you’re doing now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so, because we’ve – they’ve made sure that the course does quite a lot of things, like the business side, the multimedia side and stuff like that. I don’t know how much I’m going to use, but I’m sure some of it will be useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What are you most looking forward to about working in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I suppose doing what I want to do really. Um, I’d like to run my own thing eventually, to be able to make my own music and I’d like to do my own business side of things as well, but mainly just being able to make music, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you’re apprehensive about or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, the money side of things because it’s going to take a long time to start earning money and then paying back debts and stuff like that. It’s going to be for a couple of years really hard to cope with, money, but I’ll be all right.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Would you like to work abroad or travel at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m planning to travel when I leave here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And work at the same time, or just…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, travel for a couple of months and then work. Um, and I don’t know what kind of work I’m looking for. I think I’ll probably just work wherever and then think about a career when I come back here, but yeah I’m planning to travel next year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that the career prospects are good in music technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think they’re growing, especially in [area] and around [town] because there’s so many new studios opening up and there’s so much music coming from this part of the country. Um, London is still the place to go really if you want to work in it, because there’s so many studios there. I think the UK is good for opportunities, yeah. [Country] is not as good, I think that’s why I'm going to have to stay here, but, um, it’s quite good, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to stay around here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Around [area], yeah, I wouldn’t mind staying around here. It depends what comes up in [town] and stuff like that, but the opportunities are quite good as well, which…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m glad I decided to do this course and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think if I’d known how much multimedia was involved in this I might have chosen a different course, but I’m still glad that I did it. They’ve got new courses now, like pop music and stuff, which I probably would have chosen had I known how much multimedia was in this course, but I’m glad I did it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. I’ve nearly finished, but I’ve got a difficult question now. What five words would you use to describe like the culture or the characteristics of your field?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The characteristics of my field, like music technology?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, hard work, you need to be dedicated. Um, you need to have good personal skills with people and be creative as well; people underestimate how creative you actually need to be. Um, I think that’s it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe it as male dominated or is that –

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very male dominated, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But would that be one of the things that came into your head if you had to describe it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it would have been but I don’t even think about it any more, I’m just so used to being the only girl a lot of the time, which I don’t mind, but, yeah, it is extremely male dominated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it’ll stay like that or do you think the situation will improve for women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I think it’s going to stay like that for a while unless things are done to change the image of the course and stuff like that. But I think technology, yeah, it’s still going to stay a lot of men involved. I think bit by bit women are going to start doing it, but not for a few years I don’t think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the fact that it’s male dominated will cause you any problems in the future at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It may do. I don’t pretend that it won’t because… I just think that there is people out there who will still have preconceptions because I'm a girl that I’m going to be good at certain things and not so good at certain things. So it all depends on, I think, the attitude of your employer and the attitude of the people you work with. I think the worst way that it’s going to come across is when people expect you to be a man when they hire you or go into a studio and expect to be working with a male engineer. I think their attitudes will probably be the worst, more than an employer, to you. I just think when a band will come in, say, four males in a rock band and expect to be working with a male engineer and then I think when they see a woman they’ll be a bit like that, but not for employers I don’t think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. That’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Okay, thanks.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Thank you.
